chunks: And from him, from several of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Khalid and Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, all of them, from Uthman ibn Isa, from Sama'ah, who said:

I asked him about a man who said to his wife: 'You are separate from me' or 'You are free from me [of my dowry/obligations]', and he [the Imam] said: 'It is not [considered] anything [i.e., not a formal divorce).'

key_terms.بَائِنٌ: Separate; a term indicating separation but not necessarily formal divorce.
key_terms.بَرِيَّةٌ: Free from; often implying freedom from the husband's obligations or dowry, but not a divorce.
key_terms.لَيْسَ بِشَيْءٍ: It is not anything; a legal ruling meaning the statement does not effectuate the intended legal change (divorce).

ai.seo_question: Does saying 'you are separate from me' to one's wife constitute a divorce in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq clarifies that the phrases 'bā'in' (separate) and 'bariyyah' (free/clear) are not considered explicit divorce formulas (*zawājir*) but rather expressions of separation or freedom, thus preserving the marital bond. This ruling highlights the Shia jurisprudential emphasis on distinguishing between colloquial expressions of intent and formal legal declarations, ensuring that marriages are not dissolved inadvertently through ambiguous language.
